In the Sudans, he worked beside the African Union High Level Implementation Panel and he treated the African Union and the United Nations as two hands of one effort. Every African peacemaker who found the door of his office open and it was always open knows that partnership this partnership looked like in practice. The chairperson of the African Union Commission called him a trusted partner and a dear friend. The Secretary General named him a tireless peacemaker. Both are right. Those who served with him, as we heard from many colleagues in Juba, speak of a leader for whom human rights were daily practice and of a mentor who gave younger colleagues, many of them Africans, his time without ceremony. He carried heavy files lightly. Those of us who sat across a table from him will remember something plainer still. He listened before he spoke, and he never confused firmness with volume. He departed this world in post in March of this year and there is a rightness in the membership gathering now in the week the whole world comes to this building to say his name. The surest tribute within our search is the one, is within our reach, is the one he would have asked of us, patience, with South Sudan's peace and the practice and the persistence in it. To his family, to the people of the government of South Africa, to the people and government of South Africa, to his colleagues across the United Nations, and to all who knew him and dealt with him and benefited from him, and to the people of South Sudan whom he served until the end, the African group offers its deepest condolences. May his memory strengthen everybody in this hall who still does the quiet work of peace, and may he continue to rest in peace. I thank you.
Thank you.

Thank you, Ambassadors. Before we hear from the UN choir, we have one more poetry reading, and the poem is called "The Child is Not Dead" by Ingrid Jankers. Fink's two sisters, Chita and Lou Haysom, have asked for this poem to be read today. It will be read by Vaughn Wiles, who was at school with Fink, became a lifelong friend, and his brother-in-law, I'm told. So if I could ask Vaughn, please, to come up. Thank you.

Morning, colleagues and friends and family of Fink. I know that this was one of Fink's favorite poems. I suspect he might be listening, so I will try to do it justice. "The Child Is Not Dead" by Ingrid Jonker. The child raises his fists against his mother who screams, "Africa!" screams the smell of freedom and heather in the location of the heart under siege. The child raises his fists against his father in the march of the generations who scream Africa, scream the smell of justice and blood in the streets of armed pride. The child is not dead, neither at Lunga nor at Nyanga, nor at Orlando, nor at Sharpeville, nor at the police station in Philippi, where he lies with a bullet in his head. The child is the shadow of the soldiers, on guard with guns, saracens, and batons. The child is present at all meetings and legislations. The child peeps through the windows of houses into the hearts of mothers. The child who just wanted to play in the sun at Nyanga is everywhere. The child who became a man treks through all of Africa. The child who became a giant travels through the whole world.

Thank you. Thank you very much, Yvonne. I'd like to ask the UN Choir to make their way up here, please. We are delighted and grateful to have the UN Choir with us today. They will perform a song called "My Soul is a River." It was a piece written by composer Ben Holloway in 2004 to honor Martin Luther King for what would have been his 75th birthday. The song draws on Dr. King's favorite passage of scripture, quote, "Let justice roll down like waters and righteousness like a mighty stream," which is etched in the Civil Rights Monument in Alabama, in Montgomery. The words of this song are very apt today as we remember Fink, and I will leave you with the choir.

Thank you so much to our colleagues from the UN choir. We come to the end of this memorial. So, dear Finksters, having listened to all the speakers, I think it is clear that Fink was a cherished colleague, an inspiration, a friend, and an uncle to so many of us. And as we go on, let us keep the seeds of his humanity, his compassion, his moral courage inside all of us as we continue to work every day in the UN. May his memory be a blessing. And before we go, if you are able, I would like you to please rise for a moment of silence. Thank you very much, and I wish you all a good day. Thank you.
